titre: Lord Acton (1887): “Power Tends to Corrupt,” a Rule for Historians
accroche: Acton's sentence on absolute power comes from a private letter of 1887, and it is mostly about how to judge the powerful.
contenu_vulgarise:
“Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely.” The phrase circulates on posters, in speeches, even in textbooks, like a law of human psychology pronounced by a sage. It is actually an argument about method, written in a private letter, in a disagreement between two historians over how to judge.

## A Letter of April 5, 1887

Lord Acton, a liberal Catholic historian, wrote on April 5, 1887, to Mandell Creighton, author of a *History of the Papacy*. The letter takes a stand against the way Creighton judges great figures, popes included.

His starting point is not power in general, but a rule of judgment. He writes that he cannot accept Creighton's “canon,” according to which the pope and the king should be judged differently from other men, with a favorable presumption that they did no wrong. If there is a presumption, he says, it runs the other way, against the holders of power, and it grows with that power. The famous sentence comes right after: “Historical responsibility must make up for the absence of legal responsibility,” he writes, then “power tends to corrupt…”

## What the Sentence Says Exactly

Acton writes that power “tends” to corrupt, and that absolute power corrupts absolutely. The verb is a tendency, not a fatality: the common version, which erases it, turns a probability into a law. He adds that great men are almost always bad men, even when they exercise influence and not authority, and still more when the corruption that comes with authority is added. Further on in the same letter, he writes that there is no worse heresy than the one that makes the office sanctify its holder.

The context changes the scope of the statement. Acton is not describing a neurological mechanism or proposing a reform of institutions. He asks the historian not to absolve a man in advance because he wears a tiara or a crown. “Historical responsibility” must make up for the absence of legal responsibility: if no court can judge a king or a pope, it falls to the account given of him not to credit him without proof.

## The Shift

The sentence passes for an observation about human nature. It is first a demand on the person who writes: to distrust one's own indulgences. This also shifts the usual question. Acton is cited to say that the powerful are bad; what he asks above all is that moral judgment not stop in front of the prestige of an office, and he applies it to the popes of a Church of which he was himself a member.

There remains a difficulty he does not settle in this letter: if corruption is a tendency and not a certainty, how can one distinguish, without presuming, those it has reached from those it has spared?

repere.texte: On April 5, 1887, Acton writes to Creighton that he cannot accept judging “Pope and King unlike other men, with a favourable presumption that they did no wrong”: the presumption, if there is one, runs against the holders of power.
repere.source: Letter from Lord Acton to Mandell Creighton, April 5, 1887, Econlib (The Acton–Creighton correspondence)

carte.punch: “Power tends to corrupt”: a rule for judging the powerful (1887).
carte.idee: Acton's sentence is not a law of nature. In his letter to Creighton of April 5, 1887, it justifies a historian's rule: never presume the pope or the king innocent, because the presumption, if there is one, runs against those who hold power.

quiz.question: In the 1887 letter, what is the sentence “Power tends to corrupt…” used for?
choix: To state a law of psychology that applies to all leaders without exception
To justify not presuming the pope and the king innocent, but judging them like everyone else
To defend the idea that absolute power should be entrusted to historians
To excuse the popes of the past by recalling that the era gave them few choices
quiz.explication: Acton is answering Creighton, who wanted a favorable presumption for the great. The sentence supports a rule of method, not a natural law: the verb “tends” is a tendency, and the letter excuses no one, not even the popes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To whom does Acton address his letter of April 5, 1887?
choix: Mandell Creighton, author of a History of the Papacy
A pope he directly accuses of corruption
A newspaper that had published an anonymous article
A king he was advising on a legal reform
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Acton writes on April 5, 1887, to Mandell Creighton, author of a History of the Papacy, disagreeing with the way Creighton judges great figures, popes included.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What heresy does Acton denounce further on in the same letter?
choix: That the Church should submit to the State
That legal power should replace religious power
That the office sanctifies its holder
That historians should never judge kings
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Acton writes that there is no worse heresy than the one that makes the office sanctify its holder, targeting the favorable presumption toward the powerful.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Acton, what must historical responsibility make up for?
choix: The lack of archives on the ancient popes
The absence of religious courts in the 19th century
The absence of legal responsibility of the holders of power
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Acton writes that historical responsibility must make up for the absence of legal responsibility, for lack of a court able to judge a king or a pope.
